subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Latticework of Models
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Latticework of Models.

hook.text: Charlie Munger says having only one model is like having only one tool. Everything looks like a nail.

buildup.text: A latticework is a web of models from many fields: physics, biology, psychology, economics, and more.

discovery.text: Each model illuminates a different angle. Gravity explains orbits; incentives explain markets. Use both.

twist.text: No single discipline has all the answers. The big breakthroughs happen at the intersection of fields.

climax.text: The more models you collect and connect, the better your thinking. Breadth beats depth for judgment.

punchline.text: Many models, one mind. That's wisdom.

quiz.question: What is the latticework of mental models?
options: A web of models drawn from many disciplines
A ranking of the best models

details.summary: Charlie Munger proposed building a latticework of mental models from multiple disciplines to improve thinking. Rather than relying on one framework, combining models from psychology, economics, biology, and physics creates a richer, more accurate view of reality.
details.whyItMatters: Single-discipline thinking creates blind spots. A latticework approach helps you see connections others miss and make better decisions across domains.
takeaways: Combine models from multiple disciplines for richer thinking
No single model captures reality completely

faq.question: How many mental models does a person need?
faq.answer: Munger suggested about 80 to 90 key models spanning major disciplines. You do not need hundreds. A core set from psychology, economics, mathematics, physics, and biology covers most situations. The goal is breadth across fields, not depth in any single one.

faq.question: How do you build a latticework of mental models?
faq.answer: Read widely across disciplines. When you learn a new concept, connect it to models you already know. Practice applying models from one domain to problems in another. Over time, these connections strengthen and cross-referencing becomes automatic.
